None was a *different* Gap 338, so the number is genuinely this work's.
  - **The problem.** Gap 339 built the first destination and left `drive_archive` 422'd, so a tenant could not choose "file my approved invoices into Drive". Underneath that sat a harder problem the 422 was hiding: Feature 9's connector asks Google for `drive.readonly`, and **reading is not writing**. Pointing an upload call at the stored token would have failed with an opaque 403 for every tenant on the platform.
  - **This was a real migration, not just new code.** Scope is a property of the *grant*: a token minted under the old consent screen keeps exactly the scopes the user approved then, and **Google never widens an existing grant** when an app starts asking for more. Every `TenantConnection` row for `google_drive` created before 2026-08-30 is connected and not writable. There is no server-side fix for that — the user has to re-consent.
  - **`drive.readonly drive.file`, and specifically NOT the bare `drive` scope.** `drive` grants access to the entirety of a user's Drive; `drive.file` grants access only to files this app itself created. Asking every tenant for their whole Drive in order to drop three files in it is not a proportionate ask and was refused. `drive.readonly` stays alongside it because `drive.file` **cannot read** the tenant's existing PDFs — dropping it would have broken the Feature 9 import and the Feature 13 Autopilot sync in exchange for a write path. The bare `drive` scope is still *accepted* when detecting an existing grant (it is a superset) but never requested.
  - **The visible consequence of the narrow scope, recorded so it is not later mistaken for a bug:** the archive lands in an app-created folder named `InvoiceEQ Archive`, not in the folder the tenant picked in the connector browser. Under `drive.file` the app may only write into a folder it created itself. The alternative was full `drive` access.
  - **Re-consent is detected lazily and surfaced as an actionable state, never as a forced re-auth.** `services/workflow_outputs.py::drive_archive_readiness()` refreshes the token through the existing `get_valid_access_token()` and asks **Google's tokeninfo endpoint** what that token was actually granted (`utils/connector_oauth.py::google_granted_scopes()` / `token_has_drive_write_scope()` — plain `httpx`, matching the rest of the connector layer; `googleapiclient`/`google-auth` are not used anywhere in this backend, checked rather than assumed). It runs at exactly two moments: when `PUT /settings/workflow` is asked to store `drive_archive` (**422** naming the fix), and again before each write (logged skip, `code: "reconnect_required"` on the resolve response). A tenant that never enables the destination is never interrupted.
  - **The subtle part — three states, not two.** `token_has_drive_write_scope()` returns True/False/**None**, and `None` ("could not ask Google") is deliberately not folded into False. Refusing on an indeterminate answer would let a blip on Google's side block a tenant's configuration; so it **fails open at the probe** (`code: "scope_unknown"`, ready=True) **and fails loud at the write** — a real `403` (or `401` on a revoked token) from Drive is translated back into the *same* `reconnect_required` code rather than surfacing a raw HTTP error. One actionable state, reachable from two independent detection paths. A tokeninfo **400** (invalid/revoked token) is a definite False, not unknown.
  - **Built:** `services/workflow_outputs.py` gains the whole `drive_archive` half — `drive_archive_enabled()`, `tenant_drive_connection()`, `drive_archive_readiness()`, `_invoice_source_pdf()`, `deliver_drive_archive()`, six readiness codes; `utils/connector_files.py` gains its first write direction (`upload_google_drive_file()` — one-request `multipart/related`, so there is never a named 0-byte file in the tenant's Drive that looks like a successful archive — and `find_or_create_google_drive_folder()`); `utils/connector_oauth.py` gains the scope constants and the tokeninfo probe; `routers/connectors.py::get_auth_url()` requests the widened scope. **Reused, not rebuilt:** Gap 339's `build_invoice_csv()` / `build_invoice_json()` (the file a tenant gets in Drive and the one it gets by mail are byte-identical because they come from the same call), `export_filenames()` (refactored onto a shared `_filename_stem()`, with `export_pdf_filename()` added), `services/storage.py::download_pdf_from_storage()` for the source PDF, and `get_valid_access_token()` unchanged.
  - **Same single trigger point as Gap 339, re-confirmed rather than assumed.** `deliver_drive_archive()` is called from the same `target_status == "PAID"` block inside `routers/audit.py::resolve_audit_invoice()`, so a human clicking Approve and an `actions`-scoped API key (Gap 335) archive identically by construction — the router-level `require_actions_scope` admits both credentials and `get_tenant_or_api_key_context` normalises them before the handler body runs. Each destination gets its **own** try/except so a fault in one cannot suppress the other. A missing source PDF is isolated too: the CSV and JSON still land, with `source_pdf_included: false`.

- `[x]` **Gap 341 (BE, Feature 25 / Task 25.5): the embedded chat widget token — a chat-only credential that structurally cannot hold permissions** — built and verified 2026-08-30. Spec: [feature_25_plug_and_play_workflows.md](feature_25_plug_and_play_workflows.md) → "Gap 341 — the embedded chat widget token". Gap number collision-checked at filing time alongside Gap 340 — see that entry.
  - **What it is.** `chat_access = "widget"` has been storable since Gap 336 with no runtime effect; this builds the runtime. A widget token is pasted into **a tenant's own website's client-side code**, so it is visible in page source to every visitor, crawler and browser extension. It therefore cannot carry an API key's trust level, and the containment is **structural rather than procedural**.
  - **Its own type, and that is the security property.** `dependencies.py::WidgetContext` has exactly four fields — `tenant_id`, `widget_token_id`, `auth_method`, `origin`. **No `role`, no `key_scope`, no `db_user_id`, none of `can_train`/`can_audit`/`can_load`.** Every gate in `dependencies.py` (`require_permission`, `require_key_scope`, `require_permission_or_api_key`, `require_admin`) is annotated `context: TenantContext` and reads one of those fields, so a scope-check bug anywhere in the codebase has **nothing to check against** for a widget token — there is no field for the bug to get wrong. A test asserts the field set exactly, so adding one later fails there rather than silently widening a published credential.
  - **Its own table, and its own single mount point.** `models.py::WidgetToken` — deliberately **not** a third credential in `Tenant.api_key_hash`/`salt`/`prefix`, which are one-key-per-tenant by design and where a tenant may legitimately need several widget tokens (revoking the marketing site's must not break the docs site's). `token_prefix` is **UNIQUE** at the schema level, unlike `Tenant.api_key_prefix` which is only indexed, because it is the sole cross-tenant lookup key. `get_widget_context()` is declared in `routers/widget.py` (not in `dependencies.py`, which is where a reader goes looking for something to reuse) and **a test walks every route in the running app and asserts it is mounted on exactly one path**.
  - **Prefix dispatch made consistent across both headers.** `services/api_keys.py` gained `WIDGET_TOKEN_PREFIX`, `SANDBOX_KEY_PREFIX`, `PLATFORM_CREDENTIAL_PREFIXES` and `looks_like_platform_credential()`; `_extract_api_key()`'s Bearer test now uses it, so `Authorization: Bearer inv_widget_...` is picked up **in order to be rejected with an accurate message naming the one route it is good for**. Before, it would have fallen through to the Clerk verifier and 401'd about a token signature while the same value in `X-API-Key` 401'd about an invalid API key. `key_prefix()` became prefix-aware; **the `inv_live_` output is byte-identical** (9+6=15) and a test pins that, because `Tenant.api_key_prefix` is an indexed lookup column and moving its width would 401 every live key.
  - **CORS: a path-scoped middleware, and the global one deliberately not widened.** `main.py`'s `CORSMiddleware` runs with `allow_credentials=True`, so adding customer domains to `ALLOWED_ORIGINS` would make **every session-authenticated route in the product** cross-origin reachable, with credentials, from those domains. It was not touched — a test asserts the list still contains only first-party values. Instead `routers/widget.py::WidgetCORSMiddleware`, scoped to `/api/v1/widget`, mounted **after** the global one so Starlette makes it the outer of the two (it therefore answers preflights for unknown origins, which the inner one would pass to a 405). It reflects the request `Origin` with `Vary: Origin` and emits no credentials header.
  - **And "emit no credentials header" was not enough — a real bug, caught by a test.** Starlette's `CORSMiddleware` applies its `simple_headers` (which include `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`) to **every** response to a request carrying an `Origin`, **unconditionally, before** it decides whether that origin is allowed; only `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` is conditional. So the inner global middleware was stamping the credentials header onto widget responses, and combined with the reflected origin a browser would have been told it may send cookies cross-origin to a customer's site. `WidgetCORSMiddleware._apply()` now **deletes** the header. Caught by `test_widget_response_never_allows_credentials`, which asserts the absence **on a real response** rather than on the middleware's own output — a version checking only the latter would have passed.
  - **Origin pinning is one layer, and its limits are documented *and tested*.** `WidgetToken.allowed_origins` is checked against `Origin`/`Referer`, which browsers set and page script cannot override — so it does stop a scraped token being reused from another site. It stops nothing outside a browser (`curl -H 'Origin: …'` is the whole bypass), so it is defence-in-depth and **nothing in the code or docs claims otherwise**. `test_origin_pinning_is_bypassable_outside_a_browser` **passes by demonstrating the bypass**, so the limitation is an executable assertion rather than a comment a later reader can skip. An empty allowlist disables the layer rather than denying everything (default-deny would make every fresh token dead on arrival).
  - **One route, and it reuses the dashboard's turn.** `POST /api/v1/widget/chat/message` creates or reuses a `ChatSession` (another tenant's `session_id` is a 403, an unknown one a 404 — load-bearing when the credential is published and ids are UUIDs) and calls `routers/chat.py::run_sync_chat_turn()`, **extracted verbatim** out of `post_chat_message()`'s sync branch rather than copied. Two copies is how the quality judge and turn telemetry drift apart between dashboard and widget, and a widget turn emitting no telemetry is invisible in exactly the surface where an anonymous end user is talking to the product. Management is Admin-only on the Clerk path: `GET`/`POST`/`DELETE /api/v1/settings/security/widget-tokens[/{id}]`, shown-once, revocation effective on the next request.
  - **Also fixed here — cross-tenant chat-job read (review item 12).** `get_chat_job_status()` and `stream_chat_job()` both declared a `tenant_context` dependency and **never read it**, so any authenticated caller who learned a `job_id` could read another tenant's chat answer — reply text, generated SQL and citations, i.e. that tenant's invoice data. Every other handler in that router does the check; these two were the exception. Dormant (`ENABLE_ASYNC_CHAT_QUEUE` defaults False) and fixed anyway, **before** a credential that lives in public page source was allowed near chat. `_require_owned_chat_job()` resolves ownership through the database (`ChatMessage.job_id` → `session_id` → `ChatSession.tenant_id`), **not** the Redis blob — `enqueue_chat_job()` puts `tenant_id` there but `complete_job()`/`fail_job()` overwrite it with one that has none, so a finished job's cache cannot answer the question. Unknown ids are **404, not 403**, so the pair of responses is not a probe for which job ids exist elsewhere; and on the stream endpoint the check runs **before** the `StreamingResponse` is built, so a refusal is a 403 rather than a broken `text/event-stream`. The pre-existing `test_chat_job_status_and_stream_endpoints` **passed with no rows seeded at all**, which is precisely how the missing check stayed invisible; it was extended, not duplicated.
  - **Verification — 50 passed in 12.23s (`tests/test_widget_token.py`, new) and 13 passed (`tests/test_chat_queue.py`, 5 new cases), exit 0, nothing skipped.** Plus the shared regression runs listed under Gap 340, and `test_chat_training.py test_sse.py` → **38 passed** (the `run_sync_chat_turn` extraction and the streaming path). Breakdown in Verification Plan §16.
  - **Postgres evidence** (Hard rule 2), two cases, both **passed not skipped**. **(a) Widget token isolation** — two real tenants, two real tokens: `allowed_origins` round-tripping through real JSONB, each token resolving to its own tenant only, A's revoke not reaching B's token, a duplicate `token_prefix` raising `IntegrityError`, and an orphan `tenant_id` raising `IntegrityError`. The last two are the part SQLite structurally cannot prove (it does not enforce foreign keys by default, and `token_prefix`'s UNIQUE index is a schema constraint). **(b) The chat-job fix** — two real tenants, two real sessions, two real queued messages, `_require_owned_chat_job()` driven for all four (caller, job) combinations: each reads its own, neither reads the other's (403), unknown is 404. Postgres because the ownership answer is a two-hop join across `chat_messages.session_id` → `chat_sessions.tenant_id`, and this repo does not claim a security fix on a SQLite-only run.
  - **Migration `b1c2d3e4f5a6`** (shared with Gap 340 — one change, one revision) applied against real Postgres and **reversed and re-applied**: `alembic heads` confirmed the single head `f0a1b2c3d4e5` beforehand by a real run (Gap 60 is the multi-head incident that check exists for), columns/indexes/constraints inspected via `information_schema` and `pg_indexes`/`pg_constraint` rather than assumed, `downgrade -1` leaving `to_regclass` → `None` on both tables, and `heads` still single afterwards.
  - **Not done, not claimed.** **No FE or website surface** — no embeddable `<script>`, no Settings UI for issuing/revoking, nothing for a customer to paste (FE Gap 325). **No rate limit on the widget chat route itself** — a tenant's published token can be used by their visitors as fast as the agent answers; the sandbox meter fires here but a non-sandbox tenant is unmetered, exactly as on the dashboard. **Flagged rather than built: it is real scope and was not among the 12 approved constraints.** No CSP/`frame-ancestors` guidance shipped to tenants. No deployed run; no real browser has loaded a widget.

Maxima when the check was run: this tracker **344**, FE **341**, website **351**. (2) **346–351 are therefore holes in this tracker's local sequence**, deliberately — 352 is globally unique across all three trackers, which is the stronger guarantee, and this file already has an unused number (332).
  - **The defect.** `services/sandbox.py::charge_sandbox_chat_message()` was a read-then-decide-then-write with **no row lock and no atomic `SET col = col + 1`**: `SELECT` the `SandboxTenant` row → compare `chat_messages_used` against the limit in Python → `+= 1` → `UPDATE … SET used = <computed>`. Each chat request runs in its own session/transaction, so N concurrent requests all read the counter before any of them commits, all pass the limit check, and their increments overwrite each other. The function shipped with a comment arguing the lock was unnecessary because "the worst case of a lost update is one extra chat turn" — that holds for exactly **two** racers; for N it is **N−1 turns**, and **N is the attacker's choice**. `SANDBOX_CHAT_MESSAGE_LIMIT` (25) is the single control standing between an anonymous stranger holding an `inv_test_` key and unmetered Azure OpenAI spend that we pay for, so "not money" was wrong on its own terms.
  - **Reproduced before being fixed, on real Postgres, with production code unmodified.** A throwaway script holding a verbatim copy of the old function body, limit 5, 24 threads off a `threading.Barrier`, one `Session` per thread (one transaction per request): **22 / 19 / 24 / 24 turns allowed** across four runs, with the persisted counter finishing at **5 / 4 / 4 / 3**. Two of those runs allowed *every single request*. The counter did not just lag — it recorded fewer turns than one honest sequential run, because the lost increments were all computed from the same stale read.
  - **The fix reuses this repo's existing idiom rather than inventing one.** `locked_sandbox_select()` mirrors `services/billing_quota.py::locked_tenant_select()` exactly (statement builder exposed so a test can assert `FOR UPDATE`). `charge_sandbox_chat_message()` now: (1) an **unlocked pre-check**, purely so the common path — every ordinary tenant on every chat turn, i.e. all of them — stays lock-free; it can only ever *narrow*, since an ordinary tenant cannot become a sandbox and a claimed sandbox cannot become unclaimed; (2) `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` on the `SandboxTenant` row; (3) a **re-read under the lock** with `populate_existing=True`, load-bearing for the same reason it is in `charge_free_quota()` (Gap 343) and `claim_sandbox_tenant()` — without it SQLAlchemy answers from the identity map and the lock holds while the limit check reads stale state; (4) `claimed_at` and the limit **re-checked under the lock** (a concurrent claim or reaper delete can land after the pre-check), then increment and commit. The increment stays computed in Python rather than becoming `SET col = col + 1` deliberately: the check and the write must be **one decision**, and an atomic increment alone would still let a request past a spent allowance. The refused branch deliberately does **not** roll back — it returns into a caller that raises 402 immediately and the lock releases when the request's session closes, byte-for-byte what `charge_free_quota()` does on its own 402 branch; rolling back would give this function the power to discard a future caller's uncommitted work.
  - **Postgres evidence** (Hard rule 2), and it is a **before/after on the same database, not just a passing assertion.** Same harness, fixed function, four runs: **exactly 5 allowed, 19 refused, counter 5, overspend 0** every time. It asserts four things, not one — turns granted `== limit`, refusals `== concurrency - limit`, the persisted counter `== turns granted`, and the granted turns reporting `used` values `1..limit` **with no duplicates** (pre-fix, two callers were both told they were message 2 and three were all told message 3 — the lost-update signature). Cleans up in a `finally`; checked afterwards that every row this task created is gone.
  - **SQLite structurally cannot catch this**, which is why the fix carries two tests. SQLAlchemy's SQLite dialect renders `with_for_update()` as **nothing at all**, so a reverted fix passes there silently. `TestChatMetering::test_charge_uses_for_update` is the SQLite-safe structural half — the same assertion `tests/test_ingestion.py::test_charge_free_quota_uses_for_update` makes about `locked_tenant_select()` — and the Postgres case is the behavioural half.
  - **Verification — `tests/test_sandbox_keys.py` 52 passed in 13.69s, exit 0, nothing skipped** (50 pre-existing + 2 new; the file now has **three** real-Postgres cases). Plus `tests/test_sandbox_keys.py tests/test_widget_token.py` → **102 passed** — the widget chat route is the other caller of `charge_sandbox_chat_or_402()`. Narrow-test-per-task per this repo's standing convention.
  - **Not done, not claimed.** **No schema change and no migration** — the column already existed; the defect was that the read and the write were not one decision, so the Azure-dev backlog stays at four revisions. **No rate limit on chat itself** — this bounds a *sandbox* workspace's total turns; a signed-up tenant's chat remains unmetered, exactly as Gap 341 recorded and flagged. **Nothing else in the sandbox/widget system was touched** — in particular `scripts/sweep_sandbox_tenants.py` and every `infra/` file are untouched, because the reaper's missing ACA Job is separate, parallel work. No deployed run; local Postgres only, and `SANDBOX_KEYS_ENABLED` is still False everywhere.

Two callers landing in each other's commit/refresh window are both handed the later number and the number in between is reported to nobody. The lock's guarantee covers the decision (check + increment); it stopped at the commit, and the reported value was read after that boundary.
  - **The fix is an ordering change, three lines, no new mechanism.** Capture `charged_used = sandbox.chat_messages_used` **between the increment and the commit** — i.e. while the lock is still held — and return that local. The post-commit `refresh()` is deleted rather than kept alongside, because it is the offending read and there is nothing left for it to do: the value is already captured and the ORM instance is not used again after the return.   - **Built**: `User.can_send_invoices` (new column, migration `dfcfbb60ef1c`, `down_revision=c2d3e4f5a6b7`, single head confirmed via a real `alembic heads` run before writing it — verified up/down against a scratch table). `RoleMapper.ROLE_PERMISSION_DEFAULTS` gained the 4th key per role (`False` for every non-Admin role — Auditor included, least-privilege by design, matching this feature's existing philosophy); `resolve_permissions()` (both `models.RoleMapper` and its `dependencies.py` wrapper) and `permissions_for_key_scope()` widened from 3-tuples to 4-tuples. `TenantContext` gained `can_send_invoices: bool = False` (purely additive — every pre-existing construction site needed updating, all found via the type checker's own "cannot unpack tuple of size 4 into 3 values" errors rather than a manual audit). New `require_can_send_invoices` dependency, added as a **second, independent** `Depends()` alongside the existing `require_can_load` on `POST /outbound-invoices/upload` — both must pass; not folded into one combined check, matching this codebase's one-permission-per-dependency convention. `routers/admin.py`'s `AdminUserOut`/`PermissionsUpdate` schemas and `set_user_permissions()` gained the 4th field, defaulted (`= False`) on the update schema so an unmigrated FE build's payload still validates.
  - **`actions`-scoped API keys granted `can_send_invoices=True`**, not left at the readonly-style `False` — the founder's own documented definition of full automation (`permissions_for_key_scope()`'s docstring) explicitly named "send" as one of the automated actions, so this is consistent with the existing `can_audit`/`can_load=True` grant at that scope, not a new decision.
  - **A real bug caught by the tests, not merely avoided**: the first version of the positive "both permissions granted" test still got a 403 — turned out to be a **separate, pre-existing, unrelated check** (`upload_outbound_invoice()`'s own `if not tenant.send_invoices_enabled` guard, defaulting False on a freshly-provisioned mock tenant) firing first, not a bug in the new permission gate. Fixed the test (seed the tenant's `send_invoices_enabled=True` too, mirroring `test_outbound_ingestion.py`'s own `_seed_tenant()` pattern), not the code — the code was already correct. Also tightened the negative test's assertion from a loose `"send invoices" in detail.lower()` substring check to the exact `require_permission()` wording (`"ask an admin to grant it"`), since the tenant-flag check's *different* message also happens to contain "send invoices" and would have let a wrong-reason 403 pass silently.
  - **Verified**: `tests/test_rbac.py` + `tests/test_api_keys.py` — **77 passed** (4 new: admin-endpoint round-trip for the new field granting and revoking; outbound upload still 403s with `can_load` alone; outbound upload gets past both permission gates once both plus the pre-existing tenant flag are set; `test_scope_derives_permissions` extended to 4-tuples). Full backend suite regression covered in this session's batched final verification (see end of this file's four-gap summary). **No FE changes reflected here** — see `fe_features_tracker.md` for the Admin console checkbox / `useAuth()` / Sending-tab-visibility half.
  - Spec: `feature_1.1_rbac.md` (permission model, additive note at top) and `feature_16_settings.md` (clarifying note that the tenant-wide switch is unchanged).

- `[x]` **Gap 371 (BE): Invoice audit lifecycle has no intermediate 'Review Later' or 'Needs Resubmission' states — only PROCESSING/COMPLETED/AUDIT_REQUIRED/DUPLICATE feed into a hard PAID/REJECTED finalization** — opened 2026-09-02, sourced from an external defect review, item **General — Invoice "Review Later" & "Needs Resubmission" States** ("Expand the invoice audit lifecycle state machine to support intermediate states for disputed or queued invoices"). **Built and verified 2026-09-02.**
  - **What existed before this fix, confirmed by reading the code.** `Invoice.status` (`models.py`) defaults to `PROCESSING` and, per the extraction pipeline and Feature 7's `resolve_audit_invoice()` (`routers/audit.py`, `feature_7_audit.md`), the only values ever written were `PROCESSING → COMPLETED | AUDIT_REQUIRED | DUPLICATE` (extraction outcomes) and, via `PUT /audit/resolve/{invoice_id}`, a terminal `PAID` or `REJECTED`. No "come back to this later" or "kick back to the vendor for a corrected resubmission" state existed in the enum or the resolve endpoint.
  - **Built**: `resolve_audit_invoice()`'s status validation now accepts `REVIEW_LATER` and `NEEDS_RESUBMISSION` alongside the existing `PAID`/`REJECTED`/`AUDIT_REQUIRED`. **No database migration** — `Invoice.status` is a plain string column with no enum/CHECK constraint, so this was a pure application-logic change. Both new statuses are settable by any user who can already resolve invoices (no Admin gate, unlike Gap 193's reopen — neither undoes a prior finalization), but a new guard blocks setting either one directly on an already-terminal (PAID/REJECTED) invoice — it must be reopened (Admin-only) first, so a deferral action can never silently un-finalize an invoice. Confirmed the finalization-only side-effect blocks (webhook dispatch, staff notify, Drive archive, email summary — all keyed on `target_status in ("PAID", "REJECTED")` literally) do not fire for either new status.
  - **Inbound only in this pass, by deliberate decision**: outbound invoices (`routers/outbound_invoices.py`) have their own separate status machine (`NEEDS_REVIEW`/`VERIFIED`/`SENT`/`PAID`) with dedicated endpoints (`confirm-send`, `mark-paid`) and were not touched — extending outbound is a real follow-up, not bundled in here.
  - **FE half built in the same pass**: two new header actions ("Review Later" / "Needs Resubmission") on the Auditor Review Console (`app/invoices/review/[id]/page.tsx`), plus status badge colors — see `fe_features_tracker.md`'s own Gap 371 entry for the full FE record, including the correction of this entry's original plan (which assumed a `RecentInvoicesTable.tsx` row-actions dropdown that FE Gap 318 had already removed).
  - **Verified**: `tests/test_audit.py` — **21 passed** (5 new test functions / 9 parametrized cases): both statuses succeed from `AUDIT_REQUIRED`; both rejected from a terminal invoice with the reopen-first message; both confirmed via `assert_not_called()` to skip the PAID/REJECTED-only side effects; the 400 error message lists all five valid statuses. Full backend suite regression (this session's batched final pass, covering all four gaps): 25 failed / 1785 passed / 3 skipped / 5 deselected / 4 errors — identical failure/error set to the pre-existing baseline, zero regressions.
  - Spec: `feature_7_audit.md` (state machine and resolve endpoint, updated); related FE: `feature_4_auditor.md` (Auditor Review Console), `fe_features_tracker.md` Gap 371 entry, `feature_4.1_vendor_flow_auditor.md` (outbound dispute flow — still the natural home for a future outbound `NEEDS_RESUBMISSION`, not built here).
